input: It is important to note that pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane, where it emerges as a vapour. In this context, flux can be understood as the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour, and the separation factor can be understood as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the very same ratio in the feed. In the present comparison, two membrane types — a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane — were evaluated using a single feed consisting of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.9 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 120, whereas the zeolite membrane delivered a flux of 1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 560. Furthermore, the stability behaviour differed considerably between the two options: over the course of 500 h, the flux of the polymer membrane fell by 14%, while the flux of the zeolite membrane remained essentially unchanged over 500 h, at least within measurement error. Taken together, these results highlight an interesting trade-off between throughput, selectivity, and long-term stability. It is also worth emphasising that flux, selectivity, and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon. Finally, it should be noted that only a single feed composition was tested and that no test was extended beyond the durations described above.
target: Pervaporation separates a liquid feed across a membrane under vacuum: the feed contacts one side of the membrane and the permeating component leaves the other side as vapour. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour. The separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. Two membranes, one polymer and one zeolite, were compared on a single feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C, and each membrane was tested on the same feed, so feed composition and temperature are held fixed across the comparison. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.9 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 120; the zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 560. The polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area per hour, and the zeolite membrane enriches the permeate more strongly in water. The zeolite membrane is the more selective membrane and the polymer membrane the faster one, and a choice between the two turns on whether throughput or enrichment governs the duty. Stability separates the pair further: over 500 h the polymer flux fell 14%, while the zeolite flux was unchanged within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is limited to one feed composition, with no test run beyond 500 h.
